fields.v: Yang, C., Tian, J., Wang, Z., Liu, X., Ye, M., Chen, J. (2026). Learning Globally Reusable Skills for Coding Agents. arXiv:2608.06153v1 [cs.SE], 6 Aug 2026
Preprint — arXiv:2608.06153v1 [cs.SE], 6 Aug 2026; no published venue in the paper or access log
Tianjin University (5); Tsinghua University (Ye); industrial partner ByteDance provided data, engineers and an internal agent

Proposes an approach; secondary: Compares — GSE (globalized skill evolution with a Skill Relation Graph, cluster-based consolidation and replay-driven validation), compared with base agents, human-written skills, Live-SWE-agent and Trace2Skill on OpenHands and mini-SWE-agent, plus an industrial internal agent

GSE (version Not stated; Python, LangChain v1.1.1, DeepSeek-V4-Flash). Baselines: vanilla agent; 17 human-written skills; Live-SWE-agent (adapted to skills); Trace2Skill. Base agents: OpenHands and mini-SWE-agent (extended with skill loading), versions Not stated; plus ByteDance internal bug-triage agent

Skill bank (skills encapsulating procedural knowledge, tool schemas, constraints; general-capability and reusable-pattern skills); Skill Relation Graph (dependency, co-usage, conflict edges); DSL evolution proposals (target skill, operation, content, rationale, expected behaviour, relation updates); simplified execution traces; skill bank versioned in Git worktrees

Trace collection and simplification -> failure diagnosis (navigation/reasoning/execution) -> DSL evolution proposal with SRG-based auxiliary proposals -> local validation by replaying the failing case -> clustering and merge-agent consolidation -> replay-driven validation on historical cases -> merge into skill bank
None in GSE (fully automated evolution); human skills baseline authored by 6 senior engineers
Single artefact type (agent skill bank) learned automatically and used inside full agent runs
Not classifiable (skills are reusable procedural knowledge, not specifications of the software; authors' wording: 'skill evolution')
Existing code bases: bug-revealing unit test generation for a focal method (Java) and classification of static code-review bug reports as real or false alarm (Go)

Test generation: 108 focal methods (4-206 LOC) from 9 Java projects (Multi-SWE-Bench). False-positive filtering: IndustrialBugs, 500 reports (132 real, 368 false) from 8 repositories of 12.8-186.3 KLoC. One-project-held-out protocol
Open-source Java projects; ByteDance production Go services (RPC microservices, APIs, core business services)
N/A (automated runs); 6 senior software-quality engineers (6-10 years) wrote the human skills; reports labelled by original committers
Input, output and total tokens per case for skill evolution and for downstream task execution (macro-averaged)
Precision, recall, F1. Test generation: TP = test fails because of the ground-truth bug; FP = fails for unrelated reason; FN = no bug revealed. Filtering: prediction vs developer-confirmed label

OpenHands and mini-SWE-agent configurations (and GSE itself) all with DeepSeek-V4-Flash, temperature 0, one run. Values P / R / F1. The authors state no success criterion (no target precision, recall, F1 or token budget), so each configuration's quality and cost verdict is 'no criterion stated by the authors'.

Two tasks, one-project-held-out (evolve on other projects, test on held-out). 5 settings x 2 base agents (OpenHands, mini-SWE-agent), plus internal agent for filtering. Baseline: vanilla agent and human skills. Held constant: tools, environment, LLM (DeepSeek-V4-Flash), per-task budget, temperature 0. Acceptance: test execution against ground-truth bug; developer labels. Repetitions: 1. Human intervention: none. Leakage check: generated tests compared with reference tests (none match)

GSE best on all metrics. Test generation: F1 +40.9% (OpenHands, 0.31 vs 0.22) and +31.0% (mini, 0.38 vs 0.29) over strongest baseline; precision +6.1-27.9%, recall +31.8-64.7% (abstract ranges vs all baselines: P 6.1-34.1%, R 31.8-180.0%). Filtering: F1 0.70 vs 0.43 (OpenHands), 0.46 vs 0.39 (mini). Human skills help OpenHands but slightly hurt mini-SWE-agent on test generation. Ablations: removing SRG or generalization lowers F1. GSE uses fewer execution tokens than other skill methods (-3.3 to -4.4%) but 12.3% more evolution tokens than Trace2Skill. No significance tests

Distinguished settings, but some gaps small (e.g. precision 0.35 vs 0.33) with a single run and no variability analysis. Repeatability: temperature 0 only. Limitations of the comparison not discussed beyond threats section

Threats: generalizability across agents, languages, tasks (mitigated by two agents, Java and Go, industrial deployment); implementation errors; LLM randomness (temperature 0); data leakage (held-out projects, proprietary code). No explicit future work stated

No replication package or code link found. No pre-registration. Languages: Java (test generation), Go (filtering); GSE in Python. Tables 1-3 jumbled by pdftotext: values rebuilt by row order and checked against text deltas (p. 10, 11-12; all consistent). Abstract '61.4% F1' for industrial deployment is vs human skills; vs base 65.1%. Abstract and conclusion attribute the gains 'compared with existing evolution techniques' (P +6.1-34.1%, R +31.8-180.0% for test generation), but the lower precision end (6.1%, 0.35 vs 0.33) and the upper recall end (180.0%, 0.28 vs 0.10) come from the human-skills baseline, not from Live-SWE-agent or Trace2Skill (the other ends, 34.1% and 31.8%, are vs Trace2Skill on mini-SWE-agent: 0.55 vs 0.41, 0.29 vs 0.22); likewise the filtering recall upper end 19.8% is vs human skills on mini-SWE-agent (0.97 vs 0.81). RQ1 summary 'F1 +31.0-93.8%' is likewise vs strongest baseline and human skills. Industrial partner named ByteDance on p. 2 but anonymized later. Relevance to SDD: automatically evolved agent skill files
fields.why: The draft said the ends of the abstract's test-generation ranges come from the human-skills baseline; only two of them do (P 6.1%, R 180.0%); P 34.1% and R 31.8% are vs Trace2Skill on mini-SWE-agent (Table 1, p. 10). Added that filtering recall 19.8% is also vs human skills (Table 2, p. 12)
